analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and surgical centers to publicly report their patient infection rates.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 51 cosponsors from both parties, never got a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Hospitals Act would have required hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers to report their rates of patient-acquired infections — like MRSA and surgical site infections — to the federal government every quarter, and required the government to post that data on a public website so patients could compare facilities. It also would have let the Health and Human Services Secretary run a pilot program paying hospitals that proved they reduced infections, and imposed fines up to $10,000 on facilities that knowingly failed to report. The bill never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, especially the roughly 2 million people the bill's findings say acquire infections in hospitals and surgical centers each year, and the families of the estimated 90,000 who die from them. Public infection-rate data would let patients choose safer facilities and pressure hospitals to follow the basic hygiene and antibiotic practices the bill's findings say prevent most of these infections. Taxpayers and insurers also benefit, since the bill's findings state that infections add as much as $150,000 to a patient's bill and contribute over $50 billion in annual medical costs, much of it passed on to insurance companies and state and federal governments.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every hospital and ambulatory surgical center serving Medicare patients to report infection rates to the federal government each quarter, and requires the Health and Human Services Department to post that data on a public website in a format that lets patients compare hospitals.
Covers the major hospital-acquired infections, including surgical site infections, MRSA, central-line blood infections, urinary tract infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and C. difficile.
Requires hospitals to report patient risk factors alongside infection rates so hospitals treating sicker patients are not unfairly compared with hospitals treating healthier ones.

Authorizes a Medicare pilot program giving financial incentives or grants to hospitals that demonstrate real reductions in infection rates, capped at 10 percent of the federal savings those reductions produce.
Lets the Secretary impose civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing failure to report, and directs an annual report to Congress on infection trends, causes, and best practices.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers: they would carry the cost of quarterly data collection, face public comparison of their infection rates, and risk fines up to $10,000 for knowingly failing to report. Facilities with poor infection records would have the most to lose, since the public data would be visible to patients choosing where to get care.

drawbacks.text: Publicly comparing hospitals on infection rates is hard to do fairly: the bill tries to handle this by requiring hospitals to also report patient risk factors so the comparison accounts for how sick patients were to begin with, but crude public rankings can still penalize hospitals that treat the sickest patients.

The enforcement is light: the bill authorizes civil money penalties of no more than $10,000 per knowing failure to report, and the incentive pilot is optional and capped at 10 percent of whatever federal savings the reductions actually produce.
Hospitals would bear new quarterly data-collection and reporting costs, which could fall hardest on small critical access hospitals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: the bill's own findings cite an estimated 2 million infections and 90,000 deaths a year, over $50 billion in added medical costs, and studies showing most infections come from preventable lapses like missed handwashing and mistimed antibiotics [S3]. Public reporting is a low-cost lever that has pushed hospitals to improve in other quality areas. The main costs are hospitals' reporting burden and the risk of unfair comparisons between hospitals treating very different patients, which the bill addresses only partially through required risk-factor reporting. On balance the benefits outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to two committees; it was assigned to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever approved it or brought it to the floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 16, 2007 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
On February 27, 2007 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed.
It attracted 51 cosponsors, 29 Republicans and 22 Democrats, including the bill's original Republican sponsor joined by cosponsors of both parties.

The only further activity was three rounds of introductory remarks by the sponsor during 2007; no committee ever voted on it and the full House never debated or voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and surgical centers were better off: they never had to publicly post their infection rates or face penalties for failing to report, and patients never got the comparison data the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that avoided public infection reporting

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor joined by 29 Republican and 22 Democratic cosponsors — and the bill died without any recorded vote, so no party ever had to go on record against it.

industries.note: The bill would have required hospitals and surgical centers to report infection rates quarterly for public posting, with fines up to $10,000 for knowing failures to report — a real reputational and administrative cost. Against that, it offered voluntary pilot grants and capped incentives for hospitals that cut infections, so the sector gains on one side and is exposed on the other.

industries.industry: Health insurers and government health programs
industries.note: The bill's findings state that infection costs are passed on to insurers and governments; public reporting that drives infection rates down would reduce those added claims. This is a secondary effect and the bill does not regulate insurers directly.
